Administer
ad-MIN-is-ter
v.t. (to manage; to dispense, as a trust)
Latin administrare, to serve or manage, from ad and ministrare, to minister. The Authorized Version uses the passive twice, both in the same chapter, and both about the handling of other people's money for the poor.

Biblical Definition

Paul is gathering a large collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem, and he takes extraordinary care about who handles it. A brother is sent with Titus, “who was also chosen of the churches to travel with us with this grace, which is administered by us to the glory of the same Lord, and declaration of your ready mind” (2 Corinthians 8:19). Then he states his reason with unusual bluntness: “Avoiding this, that no man should blame us in this abundance which is administered by us” (2 Corinthians 8:20), and adds in the next verse that he provides for honest things not only in the sight of the Lord but in the sight of men. The money was not entrusted to one man, however apostolic. It travelled with a delegate chosen of the churches, so that the administration could be seen as well as done. Administration in the New Testament is a spiritual office with an accountant's discipline.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines administer as to act as minister or chief agent in managing public affairs; to dispense, as justice or a sacrament; to afford, to supply.

expand to see more

ADMINISTER, v.t. To act as minister or chief agent in managing public affairs, under laws or a constitution.

ADMINISTER, v.t. To dispense; as, to administer justice or the sacrament.

ADMINISTER, v.t. To afford, give or furnish; as, to administer relief or comfort.

STEWARD, n. A man employed to manage the domestic concerns of a family; one who is entrusted with the property of another.

ACCOUNTABLE, a. Liable to be called to account; answerable to a superior; responsible.

Key Scripture

2 Corinthians 8:19 — "And not that only, but who was also chosen of the churches to travel with us with this grace, which is administered by us to the glory of the same Lord, and declaration of your ready mind:"

2 Corinthians 8:20 — "Avoiding this, that no man should blame us in this abundance which is administered by us:"

2 Corinthians 8:21 — "Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men."

1 Corinthians 4:2 — "Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful."

Modern Corruption

Ministries routinely ask to be trusted rather than audited, treating scrutiny of money as an insult to spiritual men; Paul built his collection so that no man could blame him, and said so in writing.

expand to see more

A familiar pattern in religious fund-raising is the appeal to trust: the work is God's, the leaders are godly, and to ask hard questions about the handling of funds is treated as carnal suspicion. 2 Corinthians 8:20 is the apostolic refutation, written by a man who had every claim to be trusted on sight. He would not carry the money alone. He accepted a delegate chosen by the churches, and he stated the motive plainly — avoiding this, that no man should blame us. Paul did not merely intend to be honest; he arranged matters so that his honesty could be verified by people who did not know him.

Verse 21 gives the principle in full: providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men. Both halves are required. A man who satisfies only the second becomes a hypocrite; a man who appeals only to the first becomes unaccountable, and the history of the church is littered with the wreckage. Add to it the requirement of 1 Corinthians 4:2 — it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful — and the shape of Christian administration is clear: plural handling, open books, and delegates the churches themselves chose.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek diakoneo (G1247), to serve, to minister; diakonia (G1248), a ministry or service; charis (G5485), grace, here the collection itself; oikonomos (G3623), a steward.

expand to see more

Greek diakoneo (G1247) — to serve, to administer; the verb of 2 Corinthians 8:19-20.

Greek diakonia (G1248) — service, ministry; Paul's word for the relief collection itself.

Greek charis (G5485) — grace; the gift is called a grace administered to God's glory.

Greek cheirotoneo (G5500) — to appoint by show of hands; the brother chosen of the churches.

Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a house-manager, a steward; required to be found faithful.

Usage

"“Chosen of the churches to travel with us with this grace” — plural handling."

"“That no man should blame us in this abundance” — the stated motive."

"“Not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men” — both."
